name: TOPSY
question: Does teaching women to remove and reinsert their own vaginal pessary improve pelvic floor-specific quality of life compared with routine clinic-based pessary care?

design.population: 340 women aged 18 or older at 21 UK National Health Service pessary clinics who had retained a pessary (not shelf, Gellhorn or cube) for at least 2 weeks.
design.description: Multicenter, open-label, parallel-group superiority randomized trial
design.locator: EClinicalMedicine full text (Europe PMC), Abstract (Methods), Methods (Participants, Randomisation and masking), Results

verdictNote: No PFIQ-7 difference at 18 months; self-management had lower mean cost and fewer reported complications.
takeaway: In 340 UK women using a pessary for prolapse, taught self-management and clinic-based care gave the same 18-month PFIQ-7 score (adjusted difference −0.03 points, 95% CI −9.32 to 9.25); self-management had lower mean cost and women reported fewer pessary complications.

reports.label: 18-month report
reports.citation: Hagen S, Kearney R, Goodman K, et al. Clinical effectiveness of vaginal pessary self-management vs clinic-based care for pelvic organ prolapse (TOPSY): a randomised controlled superiority trial. *EClinicalMedicine.* 2023;66:102326.

results.measure: Pelvic Floor Impact Questionnaire-7 total score at 18 months (range 0 to 300, higher is worse), intention to treat; adjusted mean difference, self-management minus clinic-based care
results.locator: EClinicalMedicine full text (Europe PMC), Table 2; Results (Primary outcome)
results.note: Superiority not shown. Adjusted for age group, pessary user type and baseline PFIQ-7, with random intercepts for participant and centre. The authors state that the interval rules out a clinically meaningful difference, taking 20 points as the smallest meaningful difference (a consensus value; no published MCID). Baseline means were 32.5 and 31.7.

results.measure: Incremental net benefit of self-management over 18 months at a willingness to pay of £20,000 per QALY (health-sector perspective, 2019 prices)
results.locator: EClinicalMedicine full text (Europe PMC), Table 7; Abstract (Findings)
results.note: Prespecified criterion: a positive incremental net benefit implies self-management is cost-effective. Standard error £581.50; incremental cost −£150.53 and incremental QALYs 0.021; the 95% interval includes zero.

harms.label: Serious adverse events
harms.locator: EClinicalMedicine full text (Europe PMC), Results (Secondary outcomes); Abstract
harms.note: All judged unrelated to trial participation; no suspected unexpected serious adverse reactions. The abstract reports 31 events (17 and 14).

harms.label: Difficulty having sex
harms.note: Asked only of participants to whom it applied.

harms.label: Unable to remove pessary
harms.locator: EClinicalMedicine full text (Europe PMC), Table 3, footnote b
harms.note: Of the 15 self-management women unable to remove the pessary, 11 had reverted to clinic-based care.

harms.label: Difficulty removing pessary
harms.locator: EClinicalMedicine full text (Europe PMC), Table 3, footnote c
harms.note: Of the 27 self-management women with difficulty removing the pessary, 11 also reported being unable to remove it.

delivery.label: Screening and participation
delivery.value: 2514 women screened; 340 randomized (169 and 171). Randomized women were younger (64 versus 67 years) and less often existing pessary users (68% versus 80%) than eligible women who did not take part; 39% of those declining randomization had a treatment preference (33% for clinic-based care, 6% for self-management).
delivery.locator: EClinicalMedicine full text (Europe PMC), Results; Discussion

delivery.label: Sample size
delivery.value: 330 women (165 per group) for 90% power to detect a 20-point PFIQ-7 difference at 18 months (SD 50, two-sided alpha 0.05, 20% loss to follow-up).
delivery.note: The 20-point difference was a consensus value from patient representatives and clinical collaborators; no published minimal clinically important difference existed for this population.

delivery.label: Primary outcome data at 18 months
delivery.locator: EClinicalMedicine full text (Europe PMC), Results (Primary outcome)
delivery.note: 291 of 340 questionnaires (85.6%) analysed; the main reason for non-response was withdrawal (15 self-management, 8 clinic-based care).

delivery.label: Self-management intervention
delivery.value: 30-minute teaching appointment (remove, clean and reinsert under supervision), information leaflet, 2-week follow-up telephone call and a clinic telephone support number.
delivery.note: Delivered by a specialist nurse, physiotherapist or doctor trained at a site visit with a manual.

delivery.label: Clinic-based care
delivery.value: Usual appointments at which a clinician removed, cleaned and reinserted or renewed the pessary; most centres saw women every 6 months.
delivery.note: Median pessary change interval 186 days (IQR 165 to 201), excluding Covid-19 lockdown periods.

delivery.label: Pessary type at baseline
delivery.note: Shelf, Gellhorn and cube pessaries were excluded. Silicone 54/167 (32.3%) and 52/167 (31.1%); PVC 90/167 (53.9%) and 98/167 (58.7%). Mean pessary size 71.0 and 70.7 mm.

delivery.label: Baseline characteristics
delivery.value: Mean age 63.7 years; 106/340 (31.2%) new pessary users; local oestrogen 98/340 (28.8%); hysterectomy 38/340 (11.2%); previous pelvic floor surgery 39/340 (11.5%); White ethnicity 309/340 (90.9%).

delivery.label: Treatment received at 18 months
delivery.note: On treatment meant self-management teaching received and pessary insertion reported (self-management group), or no self-insertion reported (clinic group).

delivery.label: Crossover
delivery.note: Of 55 clinic-care women who said they had removed their pessary, 27 (49%) reported receiving self-management training.

delivery.label: Stopped using a pessary by 18 months
Intention to continue pessary use

delivery.label: Pessary changes found convenient
delivery.locator: EClinicalMedicine full text (Europe PMC), Results (Secondary outcomes)

delivery.label: Mean pessary-related clinic visit cost per participant
delivery.note: 2019 prices; mean total NHS cost £528.27 versus £649.63. Teaching appointment in the self-management group costed at a mean £31.77 (n=125).

reports.label: 4-year follow-up
reports.citation: Bugge C, Kearney R, Best C, et al. Four year clinical and cost effectiveness of vaginal pessary self-management versus clinic-based care for pelvic organ prolapse (TOPSY): long term follow-up of a randomised controlled superiority trial. *BJOG.* 2025;132(12):1762-1771.

results.measure: PFIQ-7 total score at 4 years, intention to treat; adjusted mean difference, self-management minus clinic-based care
results.locator: BJOG full text (PMC12501713), Table 1; Results (Primary outcome)

results.measure: Equivalence test at 4 years against the 20-point minimal clinically important difference (added because the 18-month result was null)
results.locator: BJOG full text (PMC12501713), Methods (Statistics); Results (Primary outcome)
results.note: The null hypothesis of a 20-point difference was rejected (t[184] = 2.317).

results.measure: Incremental net benefit of self-management at 4 years at a willingness to pay of £20,000 per QALY (health-sector perspective, 2019/2020 prices)
results.note: Bootstrapped standard error £1530.25; incremental cost −£239.06 (SE £176.44) and incremental QALYs 0.100 (SE 0.073). Probability of cost-effectiveness 92.97% at £20,000 per QALY. Complete-case sample of 169 (excluded 17).

results.measure: Mean percentage of applicable complication types reported per participant over the previous 6 months at 4 years; adjusted mean difference (positive when the self-management rate is lower)
results.locator: BJOG full text (PMC12501713), Table 2; Results (Secondary outcomes)
results.note: The report labels differences self-management minus clinic-based care but gives a positive value with the lower rate in the self-management group, so the sign here is read as clinic-based minus self-management. The abstract prints the self-management mean as 17.7%.

results.measure: Prolapse surgery between randomization and 4 years among responders
results.locator: BJOG full text (PMC12501713), Results (Pessary Use and Care Pathways)
results.note: Eight of 186 responders (4%) had any surgery: 4 prolapse surgery, 1 incontinence surgery and 3 hysterectomy.

harms.label: Serious adverse events between 18 months and 4 years
harms.note: One possibly related event, in the self-management group (urinary and chest infections with hospitalization); all others unrelated.

delivery.label: Responders at 4 years
delivery.note: 186 of 340 women (55%) opted in and returned a questionnaire; the report found no substantial differences in baseline characteristics between responders and non-responders.

delivery.label: Care after the 18-month trial period
delivery.value: At 18 months clinical care returned to each centre; women could self-manage or attend clinic according to local practice and preference.

delivery.label: Self-management among current pessary users at 4 years

values.exp: 60/75 (80%) still self-managing (15 had changed to clinic-based care)

delivery.locator: BJOG full text (PMC12501713), Results (Pessary Use and Care Pathways)
delivery.note: Half of the original self-management responders (43) and 45 (45%) of the clinic-based responders reported self-management training since 18 months.
